Canada workers benefit 2026: the phase-in, the 15% phase-out, a second earner and the advance payments

A worked guide to the 2026 Canada workers benefit (CWB): how the basic amount and disability supplement build up and phase out, what a pay rise or a spouse’s new job really changes, why an RRSP deduction can raise the benefit, and how ACWB advances reconcile at filing. Six charts and an editable 2026 model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test the 2026 Canada workers benefit phase-in, phase-out and advance payments

The central idea

The CWB adds 27 cents per dollar earned above CAD 3,000 until it reaches its maximum, then removes 15 cents per dollar of adjusted net income above the threshold. Inside the phase-out a raise is worth less than it looks, a lower-earning spouse is partly shielded by the secondary earner exemption, and advances based on last year’s return can turn into a repayment.

01

Two refundable pieces: the basic amount and the disability supplement

The Canada workers benefit is a refundable tax credit for people with working income and low net income. It has a basic amount and, for people eligible for the disability tax credit (an approved Form T2201 on file), a disability supplement. Because it is refundable, it is paid even when no income tax is owing; it is claimed on Schedule 6 and line 45300 of the return.

To qualify for the basic amount, the CRA requires working income, net income below the threshold for the province or territory, Canadian residence for the whole year, and age 19 or older on 31 December—or living with a spouse, common-law partner or child. Full-time students at a designated institution for more than 13 weeks are excluded unless they have an eligible dependant, as are people confined to a prison or similar institution for at least 90 days in the year and people exempt from Canadian tax as officers or servants of another country. The same exclusions apply to the spouse.

“Family” here means a person with an eligible spouse or common-law partner or an eligible dependant (a child under 19 living with them on 31 December who is not eligible for the CWB). Residents of Alberta, Quebec and Nunavut have reconfigured amounts under agreements with the federal government; they are not modelled.

02

Where the 27% and 15% come from—and the three zones they create

Section 122.7 of the Income Tax Act sets the mechanics; the dollar amounts in it are indexed each year. The basic amount is the lesser of the maximum and 27% of working income above CAD 3,000 (combined working income for a family), minus 15% of adjusted net income above the phase-out threshold (adjusted family net income for a family). The disability supplement is the lesser of its maximum and 27% of the eligible person’s working income above CAD 1,150, minus 15% of adjusted net income above its own, higher threshold. When both spouses are eligible for the disability tax credit, each supplement is reduced at 7.5%.

That gives three zones for a single person in 2026. From CAD 3,000 to about CAD 9,167 of working income the benefit grows 27 cents per dollar. Between there and CAD 27,392 of adjusted net income it stays at CAD 1,665. Above CAD 27,392 it falls 15 cents per dollar and is gone at CAD 38,492. Working income is employment and business income; adjusted net income starts from net income, so employment insurance, interest or pension income raise it without adding working income, while RRSP and FHSA deductions lower it without reducing working income.

The marginal-rate chart shows the same thing as a rate: the CWB effectively pays 27% on extra earnings in the phase-in and charges 15% in the phase-out, on top of income tax and payroll contributions.

03

Worked example: a CAD 2,000 raise at CAD 30,000 keeps CAD 1,420 before other deductions

Jordan is single, has no children and expects CAD 30,000 of employment income in 2026 with no other income or deductions. Adjusted net income is CAD 30,000, which is CAD 2,608 above the CAD 27,392 threshold, so the basic amount is CAD 1,665 − 15% × 2,608 = CAD 1,273.80.

A CAD 2,000 raise lifts adjusted net income to CAD 32,000. The benefit becomes CAD 1,665 − 15% × 4,608 = CAD 973.80, so CAD 300.00 of the raise disappears into the phase-out. Applying the 2026 lowest federal bracket rate of 14% removes another CAD 280.00, leaving CAD 1,420.00. Provincial tax and CPP and EI contributions would take more; the model lets you enter whatever combined rate you want to test instead of the 14% default.

The same arithmetic runs in reverse for deductions. If Jordan earns the CAD 32,000 and contributes CAD 2,000 to an RRSP and deducts it, adjusted net income returns to CAD 30,000 and the CWB returns to CAD 1,273.80—a CAD 300.00 benefit gain on top of the income-tax saving from the deduction. A CAD 3,000 deduction at CAD 30,000 brings adjusted net income to CAD 27,000 and restores the full CAD 1,665. This is one of the few places where a modest RRSP or FHSA deduction has a 15% benefit effect for a low-income worker; whether the deduction is worth more later is a separate question covered in the related RRSP timing guide.

04

A spouse’s new job: the secondary earner exemption delays the phase-out

For a couple, the phase-in uses combined working income and the phase-out uses adjusted family net income. Without a special rule, a second earner’s first dollars would be clawed back at 15% as soon as the family crossed CAD 31,251. Section 122.7(1.3) prevents part of that: the lower earner’s adjusted net income is reduced by the lesser of their working income and the secondary earner exemption, CAD 16,714 for 2026.

Hypothetical example: Morgan earns CAD 28,000 and Casey starts a part-time job paying CAD 12,000. Combined working income is CAD 40,000, which fully phases in the CAD 2,869 family maximum. Casey’s CAD 12,000 is below the exemption, so adjusted family net income stays at CAD 28,000—below the threshold—and the family keeps the full CAD 2,869. Without the exemption, family income of CAD 40,000 would cut the benefit by CAD 1,312.35 to CAD 1,556.65. The second-earner chart traces that gap as the spouse’s earnings rise: the two lines separate once family income crosses the threshold and run parallel, CAD 2,507.10 apart, once the exemption is fully used at CAD 16,714 of spouse earnings, until the exemption line also reaches zero.

The exemption applies to the lower earner only and only to working income. Employment insurance, pension or investment income received by either spouse counts in full.

05

The disability supplement phases out later—and more slowly for two eligible spouses

The supplement starts at a lower floor (CAD 1,150 of the eligible person’s own working income) and reaches its CAD 860 maximum at about CAD 4,335. Its phase-out begins only at CAD 38,495 of adjusted net income for a single person and CAD 50,377 for a family, so it often survives after the basic amount has gone.

For a single person with the disability tax credit and CAD 20,000 of working income, the model gives the full basic amount of CAD 1,665 plus the full CAD 860 supplement: CAD 2,525. For a couple who both qualify, each person has a supplement based on their own working income and each is reduced at 7.5% rather than 15% above CAD 50,377. With CAD 40,000 and CAD 20,000 of working income, the secondary earner exemption brings adjusted family net income to CAD 43,286: the basic amount is CAD 2,869 − 15% × 12,035 = CAD 1,063.75, both supplements remain at CAD 860, and the family total is CAD 2,783.75.

06

Advance payments: half the credit early, settled on the return

Since the Advanced Canada workers benefit (ACWB) began, eligible people receive up to 50% of their CWB in advance without applying; the CRA determines eligibility from the tax return, which must be received before 1 November of the July–June benefit period. Couples receive the basic advance through one spouse—the one with the higher working income, or the first to file if incomes are equal—and a spouse eligible for the disability tax credit receives their own supplement advance. CRA’s benefit-payment calendar (page dated 14 October 2026) lists ACWB dates of 12 January 2026, 10 July 2026 and 9 October 2026; the CRA’s claim page gives the pattern as 12 July, 11 October and 10 January, moved earlier when the date falls on a weekend or holiday.

The advance is an estimate, not the entitlement. It is reported on an RC210 slip; the full CWB is claimed on line 45300 and the advances are entered through Schedule 6 on line 41500, so only the difference affects the refund or balance owing. In the default scenario Jordan received CAD 816.50—half of the CAD 1,633 2025 maximum Jordan qualified for in the prior year—and is entitled to CAD 1,273.80 for 2026, so CAD 457.30 arrives through the return. If Jordan’s income had climbed to CAD 40,000, the 2026 entitlement would be zero and the CAD 816.50 would be repaid. Only death, incarceration or emigration change advances during the year; other changes take effect only after a reassessment.

Which payments belong to which year’s slip should be read from the RC210 itself. The model simply takes the advances you enter for the year and subtracts them.

07

A planning checklist and the limits of this model

  • Locate the zone first. Below the maximum, extra work increases the CWB; in the plateau it has no effect; in the phase-out every extra dollar of net income costs 15 cents (7.5 cents per supplement for two eligible spouses).
  • Count the whole stack. In the phase-out, the CWB, income tax, CPP and EI contributions, the GST/HST credit, provincial benefits and the Canada child benefit can all respond to the same dollar. The model only adds the one rate you enter.
  • Use deductions deliberately. RRSP and FHSA deductions lower adjusted net income; union dues and child-care expenses also reduce net income. Their benefit effect depends on where the household sits on the curve.
  • Plan for the advance true-up. If income is rising, keep part of each ACWB payment until the return is assessed.
  • Confirm eligibility. Age, full-year residence, student status, incarceration and province all decide whether these figures apply at all.

The interactive model covers the 2026 federal CWB outside Alberta, Quebec and Nunavut. It treats all working income as also counting in net income, ignores the section 122.7(1.1) election for tax-exempt employment income of registered Indians, and does not model the special rules when a spouse dies after 30 June. It is a teaching tool for the mechanics, not a filing or entitlement calculation.
